newsitem.title: USA: Fed's Greenspan says U.S. bank laws need updating.
newsitem.headline: Fed's Greenspan says U.S. bank laws need updating.

text.p: Regulators can only go so far to update the U.S. banking environment and ultimately Congress needs to act on outdated laws, Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan said Saturday.

The Fed has attempted to modify its regulations in the area of securities powers permitted for bank holding companies. The Fed has proposed raising the limit on the amount of securities underwriting that a bank's securities unit, known as a section 20 subsidiary, can conduct in areas such as stocks and corporate bonds.

"Most recently, based on our favorable experience with these subsidiaries, we have proposed dismantling some of the limitations and restrictions that, in an abundance of caution, we originally imposed to constrain risk exposures of the insured bank affiliate," Greenspan said in a speech to an American Bankers Association convention.
The Fed has also proposed "a wide ranging revision" of its Regulation Y to streamline the bank holding company application process, he said.
The proposed regulatory changes, however, highlight a major problem in that both areas are "constrained by outdated and increasingly inefficient statutes," Greenspan said.

"Indeed, statutory provisions ultimately limit the Fed's ability to relax Section 20 or Regulation Y limits," he said. "Fundamental congressional reform of the Glass-Steagall and the Bank Holding Company Acts is still needed," Greenspan said.

Glass-Steagall is a Depression-era law that separates investment and commercial banking. Attempts in the 104th Congress, that ended this week, to repeal the law fell through and the next Congress is expected to try again.
Greenspan also warned that banks unwilling to adapt to technological change and competition "will lose market share and suffer lower risk-adjusted rates of return."

"Because the hot hand of competition is always putting pressure on us, we in our darker moments wish it would just go away," the Fed chairman said. "I very often succumbed to such melancholy when I was in the private sector. But we are wrong," he added.
"Competition is the force which keeps us on our toes, makes us better and more productive," Greenspan said.

The goal is not to have a zero failure rate for banks, because risk-taking means that failures will occur and without risk-taking the banking system would not be in a position to foster economic growth, he said.
However, regulators are watchful of how banks manage risk and risk-management standards are increasingly an important supplement to traditional supervisory techniques, Greenspan said.

"It does not matter whether the bank concentrates on low- risk, low capital business, or on high-risk, high capital business, only that it concentrates on businesses for which it has a comparative advantage," he said.
That would be businesses that earn an above average rate on the bank's internally allocated capital, after provisions for expected losses, Greenspan said.
